name: Eddy currents
description: A metal plate alone in your solenoid, whose field now swings back and forth, $B = B_0 \sin \omega t$. A changing magnetic field induces an electric field that circulates about the solenoid's axis (Faraday's law), and in the metal it drives the carriers round in loops: eddy currents, which heat it, the faster the field changes the more (as $\dot B^2$). Set the swing $B_0$ so that the plate takes between 1.2 and 4 of heat per unit time (averaged over $t = 25$ to $125$).

reality.represents: Eddy currents heating a conducting plate

remarks.detail: The changing field induces a circulating electric field, which drives the carriers round in loops; the heat grows as Ḃ², as the torsion-function law gives.
Here the field turns the carriers' paths by a good part of a radian between collisions (ω_c τ ≈ 0.4): a semiconductor's regime; in copper it barely turns them (Eddy currents in silicon).

The carriers' currents make no magnetic field of their own: no self-inductance and no skin effect, valid while the skin depth is far larger than the conductor. The only magnetic field is the solenoid's.

remarks.line: A classical metal, a semiconductor by its ratios
remarks.detail: The carriers are classical particles at the lattice's temperature bouncing off fixed ion cores (the Drude model). A real metal's electrons are a degenerate quantum gas whose own ratios (plasma oscillations per collision, screening per free path) the model cannot afford; its carriers have a lightly doped semiconductor's ratios (the Scales section names which), which conducts by the same laws.

electrodes.label: inert electrode (floating, emits nothing; the model needs one)
